title: Knowledge check: SQL Injection Prevention

questions.prompt: Which subtopic is explicitly listed under “SQL Injection Prevention” in the attached Classic ASP curriculum?
questions.explanation: The PDF lists “How SQL injection occurs” under lesson 93, “SQL Injection Prevention”. The distractors belong to other lesson topics.

questions.prompt: When applying “SQL Injection Prevention” in a legacy Classic ASP application, which approach is strongest?
options: Hide the button but leave the endpoint unprotected.
Return internal diagnostics to every browser.
Enforce the control on the server and verify a denial/failure case.
questions.answer_key: Enforce the control on the server and verify a denial/failure case.
questions.explanation: This approach keeps sql injection prevention testable and respects Classic ASP/IIS runtime boundaries. The exact IIS, provider, or component behavior must be checked in the target test environment.

questions.prompt: Before marking work on “SQL Injection Prevention” ready for review, what evidence should be recorded?
options: Delete diagnostic evidence before recording the outcome.
Treat a successful happy-path test as proof of all security properties.
Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
Claim the production deployment passed without running it.
questions.answer_key: Document the observed result, tool/runtime version, and one meaningful failure or edge case.
questions.explanation: Good maintenance evidence includes the expected and observed result, relevant version/runtime assumptions, and a boundary or failure test. Never claim an execution/deployment test that was not run.
